title: Codeword search with random hash constraints
problem_latex: For security parameter $\lambda$, fix the folded Reed--Solomon code $C_\lambda\subseteq\Sigma^n$ from Lemma 4.2, where $n=\Theta(\lambda)$ and $|\Sigma|=2^{\lambda^{\Theta(1)}}$. Given oracle access to $H:\Sigma\to\{0,1\}^n$, output $c\in C_\lambda$ satisfying $H_i(c_i)=1$ for every coordinate $i$. This NP search relation has a publicly checkable witness. Complexity uses random-oracle queries and gates; $H_i$ denotes output bit $i$.
quantum_latex: $\operatorname{poly}(\lambda)$ gates and at most $n\lambda$ quantum queries, by Yamakawa--Zhandry, with success $1-\operatorname{negl}(\lambda)$ over random $H$. Prepare the code superposition and coordinate states supported on $H_i^{-1}(1)$, Fourier transform both, coherently add and decode the dual code, then inverse transform. Verification uses $n$ classical hash queries and polynomial code-membership work. A salted two-message construction handles nonuniform provers.
classical_latex: For fixed $0<c<c'<1$ in the code construction, every computationally unbounded classical algorithm using at most $2^{\lambda^c}$ oracle queries succeeds with probability at most $2^{-\Omega(\lambda)}$ (Lemma 6.9). Random codeword trials provide an $O(n2^n)$-query exponential comparator on typical random oracles. The keyless bound concerns uniform algorithms; the keyed construction treats oracle-dependent advice. Substituting an explicit cryptographic hash makes hardness an assumption about that family.

title: Interactive proofs of quantumness
problem_latex: A classical verifier supplies a public key for a trapdoor claw-free pair $(f_{k,0},f_{k,1})$. The prover commits to an image $y$, then answers a random challenge with a preimage or a prescribed measurement relation between its two preimages. The objective is an acceptance probability above the efficient-classical-prover threshold. Complexity uses gates, communication, and security parameter $\lambda$.
quantum_latex: $\operatorname{poly}(\lambda)$ prover gates and verifier time. Coherent function evaluation and image measurement retain a superposition of the two preimages. BCMVV uses complementary-basis challenges. The computational Bell protocol achieves $p_x=1$ and $p_{\rm CHSH}=\cos^2(\pi/8)$; Rabin-function implementations use modular squaring.
classical_latex: Under claw-freeness, classical polynomial-time provers satisfy $p_x+4p_{\rm CHSH}-4\leq\operatorname{negl}(\lambda)$. For the factoring-based instantiation, factoring the $\lambda$-bit modulus gives an attack with heuristic number-field-sieve time $\exp(O(\lambda^{1/3}(\log\lambda)^{2/3}))$. The LWE instantiation uses its lattice-attack parameters and adaptive-hardcore-bit assumption.

title: Classical verification of quantum computation
problem_latex: Given a quantum circuit deciding a promise problem with completeness at least $2/3$ and soundness at most $1/3$, construct an interactive protocol with a classical polynomial-time verifier and a quantum polynomial-time honest prover certifying the decision. Security is against efficient quantum cheating provers. Complexity uses gates, verifier time, and classical communication.
quantum_latex: $\operatorname{poly}(T,\lambda)$ gates for circuit size $T$ and security parameter $\lambda$, using Mahadev's four-message protocol. Cryptographic commitments enforce computational- or Hadamard-basis measurements; the verifier checks a computation-verification test.
classical_latex: The verifier runs in $\operatorname{poly}(T,\lambda)$ classical time. A classical honest prover for every BQP computation would require classical algorithms for those computations; generic simulation and problem-specific algorithms supply their respective comparators. Protocol soundness reduces to quantum hardness of LWE.

title: Certified randomness from an untrusted quantum device
problem_latex: A classical verifier interacts with an untrusted device and outputs $Z$ with conditional smooth min-entropy $H_{\min}^{\varepsilon}(Z\mid E,\mathrm{transcript})\geq k$, for the side information $E$ admitted by the protocol. A seeded extractor gives nearly uniform bits. Complexity counts prover gates, communication, verification, and certified entropy.
quantum_latex: BCMVV uses polynomially many cryptographic rounds to certify entropy under LWE-based assumptions. A separate random-circuit protocol executes challenged circuits and classically checks selected probabilities. Its 2025 experiment certified $71{,}313$ entropy bits with 56 trapped-ion qubits under a restricted-adversary model.
classical_latex: A classical device can retain every output, yielding zero conditional entropy against its own side information. The circuit-based protocol bounds the number of samples obtainable by a time-limited classical adversary; its verification used combined sustained performance $1.1\times10^{18}$ floating-point operations per second.

title: Random circuit sampling
problem_latex: Given an $n$-qubit circuit $U$ with $g$ gates from a specified ensemble, sample $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ from $p_U(x)=|\langle x|U|0^n\rangle|^2$, exactly or within total variation distance $\varepsilon$. Geometry, gate distribution, and noise define the instance family. Complexity uses gates and classical sampling time.
quantum_latex: $O(g+n)$ operations per ideal sample by direct circuit execution and measurement. Finite-gate-set compilation adds its precision overhead.
classical_latex: Use the minimum of state-vector simulation $O(g2^n)$, tensor contraction $\operatorname{poly}(g)2^{O(w)}$ at contraction width $w$, and fixed-algebraic-gate path counting $\operatorname{poly}(s)2^{O(s/\sqrt{\log s})}$ for a sparse Boolean encoding of size $s$ of the required marginal. Sequential conditional probabilities give samples with polynomial overhead. Constant-rate noisy random circuits in the anticoncentration regime admit polynomial-time approximate classical sampling.

title: Fock-state boson sampling
problem_latex: Given an $m\times m$ interferometer $U$ and single photons in $n\leq m$ specified inputs, sample $s\in\mathbb N^m$, $\sum_i s_i=n$, with $p(s)=|\operatorname{Per}(U_s)|^2/\prod_i s_i!$. Matrix $U_s$ uses occupied input columns and repeats row $i$ exactly $s_i$ times. Complexity uses optical operations and classical arithmetic time at specified precision.
quantum_latex: $O(m^2)$ two-mode optical elements implement a general interferometer, followed by photon-number detection. Scattershot boson sampling varies the occupied input modes.
classical_latex: Clifford--Clifford exact sampling costs $O(n2^n+mn^2)$. Their collision-aware algorithm has Haar-average bound $O(\frac{n(m+n)}m\frac{\binom{2m+n}{n+1}}{\binom{m+n}{n+1}}+n^2m)$. For fixed nonzero uniform loss, the November 2026 loss theorem gives polynomial approximate sampling with total-variation error averaged over Haar interferometers.

title: Gaussian boson sampling
problem_latex: Given a complex symmetric $B$ with singular values below one, sample $s\in\mathbb N^m$ with $p(s)=\sqrt{\det(I-BB^\dagger)}|\operatorname{Haf}(B_s)|^2/\prod_i s_i!$, where $B_s$ repeats row and column $i$ exactly $s_i$ times. This is discrete photon-number sampling from a pure zero-mean Gaussian state. Complexity uses optical operations and classical sampling time.
quantum_latex: $O(m^2)$ optical elements, $m$ squeezed input modes, and photon counting implement a general instance. Total detected photon count $N=\sum_i s_i$ is a random output parameter controlled by squeezing.
classical_latex: Conditional heterodyne sampling and loop-hafnian evaluation cost $O(mN^3 2^{N/2})$ for an $N$-photon output, with the numerical cutoff specified. Polynomial classical samplers cover the nonnegative graph distributions in Anand et al. Equal bounded squeezing and fixed uniform loss admit polynomial sampling with Haar-average total-variation accuracy by the 2026 loss theorem.

title: Normalized trace estimation for a quantum circuit
problem_latex: Given an $n$-qubit unitary circuit $U$ of size $g$, estimate both components of $2^{-n}\operatorname{Tr}(U)$ to additive error $\varepsilon$ with failure probability $\delta$. The input is a succinct circuit. Complexity uses gates and classical time; the problem characterizes DQC1.
quantum_latex: $O(g\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$ gates by Knill--Laflamme. A clean control applies controlled-$U$ to $I/2^n$; its $X$ and $Y$ expectations give the trace.
classical_latex: Random-vector trace estimation with state-vector circuit application costs $O(g2^n\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))$. Tensor contraction provides width-dependent alternatives. For fixed finite algebraic gates, trace path counting also costs $\operatorname{poly}(s)2^{O(s/\sqrt{\log s})}$ in the size $s$ of its sparse Boolean encoding.

title: Two-dimensional hidden linear function
problem_latex: On an $n$-vertex square grid, input bits $A_e,b_v$ define $q(x)=2\sum_{e=\{u,v\}}A_ex_ux_v+\sum_v b_vx_v\pmod4$. Let $L_q=\{x:q(x\oplus y)=q(x)+q(y)\ \forall y\}$. Output $z\in\mathbb F_2^n$ with $q(x)=2z^Tx$ for every $x\in L_q$. Complexity counts bounded-fan-in circuit depth.
quantum_latex: $O(1)$ depth and $O(n)$ gates on a nearest-neighbor grid: apply $H^{\otimes n}$, the Clifford phase $i^{q(x)}$, and $H^{\otimes n}$. Every measured output satisfies the relation. An encoded construction extends the separation to a related noisy three-dimensional task.
classical_latex: $\Omega(\log n)$ depth for bounded-fan-in randomized classical circuits solving all instances with the stipulated success probability. Stabilizer simulation or finite-field linear algebra gives polynomial sequential time; parallel linear algebra gives polylogarithmic depth.

title: Equality in simultaneous-message communication
problem_latex: Alice receives $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ and Bob receives $y\in\{0,1\}^n$. Each sends one message to a referee deciding $x=y$ with error at most $1/3$. The senders have independent private randomness and no shared random key or prior entanglement. Complexity counts transmitted bits or qubits.

classical_latex: $\Theta(\sqrt n)$ bits for bounded-error private-coin simultaneous-message protocols. Classical fingerprints sample codeword positions; matching lower bounds apply in the same model.

title: Hidden matching in one-way communication
problem_latex: Alice holds $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ and Bob a perfect matching $M$ on $[n]$. After one message from Alice, Bob outputs an edge $(i,j)\in M$ and the bit $x_i\oplus x_j$, with success at least $2/3$. Complexity counts one-way communicated bits or qubits.
quantum_latex: $\lceil\log_2n\rceil$ qubits with exact success. Alice sends $n^{-1/2}\sum_i(-1)^{x_i}|i\rangle$; Bob measures in the basis $(|i\rangle\pm|j\rangle)/\sqrt2$ for edges in $M$.
classical_latex: $\Omega(\sqrt n)$ randomized classical bits are necessary. Shared randomness enables a matching $O(\sqrt n)$ birthday-paradox protocol; sending sampled indices explicitly costs $O(\sqrt n\log n)$ with private randomness.

title: Hidden subgroup identification in a general finite group
problem_latex: Given finite $G$ and an oracle $f:G\to X$ constant on, and distinct between, the left cosets of unknown $H\leq G$, output generators of $H$. Complexity counts oracle queries; $n=\lceil\log_2|G|\rceil$.
quantum_latex: $O(n^2+\log(1/\delta))$ queries with error $\delta$ by the Ettinger--H{\o}yer--Knill subgroup-state test. An exact construction uses $O(n^4)$ queries with arbitrary one-qubit gates. General subgroup discrimination and preprocessing require exponential resources.
classical_latex: Repeated birthday-collision sampling finds generators with $O(n2^{n/2})$ queries in the worst case; equal oracle values give elements of $H$. Simon-type order-two subgroups require $\Omega(2^{n/2})$ randomized queries. For finite abelian groups, subgroup-sensitive identification costs $O(\sqrt{(|G|/|H|)\log|H|}+\log|H|)$ deterministic queries.

title: Exact leader election in anonymous networks
problem_latex: In a connected synchronous network of $n$ identical processors without unique identifiers, each knows $n$. Output bits summing to exactly one, in bounded time with zero error, on every topology. Complexity counts rounds and transmitted bits or qubits.
quantum_latex: $O(n)$ rounds and $O(mn^2)$ communication for $m$ links by Kobayashi--Matsumoto--Tani. Coherent symmetric-function computation enables exact symmetry breaking.
classical_latex: Exact bounded-time leader election is impossible on general anonymous classical networks even with known n. Symmetric executions on symmetric topologies keep processors indistinguishable.

title: Mermin--Peres magic-square game
problem_latex: A referee independently samples row $r\in\{1,2,3\}$ for Alice and column $c\in\{1,2,3\}$ for Bob. Alice outputs three signs of product $+1$ and Bob three of product $-1$; their intersection values must agree. No communication follows the inputs. Complexity uses winning probability and shared entanglement.
quantum_latex: Success $1$ with two EPR pairs and constant-size local measurements. Commuting Mermin--Peres observables supply the required parities and agreement.
classical_latex: Optimal classical success is exactly $8/9$, allowing shared randomness and arbitrary local computation. A deterministic assignment satisfying eight of nine input pairs attains it.
